About 700 species worldwide, temperate to tropical regions
Peninsular Malaysia has 29 species, including nine endemics.

Most species occur in damp shaded forest understorey, forest gaps and secondary forests; a few survive also on moist rock faces or crevices, such as on limestone hills; and a number of montane species even thrive in forest edges and open sites in the cool climate

Many species are frequently found carpeting the ground in forests, sometimes colonising entire earth banks; their easy growth from vegetative fragments and frequent production of spores no doubt assist in fast reproduction

Species of wide ecological amplitude include Selaginella intermedia, S. roxburghii and S. wallichii (lowlands to montane forest, moist valleys to dry forested hill ridges), and S. alutacia (lowlands to montane forest, but only moist sites)
As far as is known, no species is endemic to limestone in Peninsular Malaysia
Selaginella willdenowii is the only climbing species, scrambling over vegetation by means of long relay-stems to several metres long, sometimes even forming thickets
Sing. 30 (1977) 21--29) has investigated the potential advantage of a metallic blue tinge often developing in leafy sprays of S. willdenowii
This iridescence is not due to pigmentation

It is the reflective property of the leaf surface, which behaves as an interference filter mainly reflecting blue wavelengths, and transmitting through the photosynthetic tissue the higher wavelengths (in the red region) that predominate in diffuse light reaching the rain forest floor
Apparently, as in many shade-tolerant plants, iridescent leaves have more chlorophyll per unit protein than leaves exposed to the sun
On some lawns in the lowlands around Kuala Lumpur, regular grass-cutting has helped the proliferation of the creeping S. mayeri, which manages to become persistent in turf interstices
Selaginella intermedia and S. roxburghii are spontaneously occurring, non-aggressive and permissible ground cover elements in some rubber and oil palm plantations.
Many species, such as Selaginella frondosa, have good potential as horticultural elements in gardening, giving good bedding or edging material for ground plantings and potted specimens
The frequently reddish stems in many species, and characteristic silvery-grey or variously coppery to pink leafy sprays of S. argentea and S. intermedia, respectively, make them attractive
The blue-green coloration in fronds of shade-grown S. willdenowii is particularly notable

Selaginella tamariscina (Beauv.) Spring, not native in Peninsular Malaysia but distributed from Siberia southward to Thailand, the Philippines, islands off the north Borneo coast (including dry, exposed volcanic rims) and Lombok has been introduced as an aquarium plant, as have various other forest selaginellas at random

Selaginella tamariscina has erect lower stem portions and rhizophores that loosely bunch forming a false trunk (giving ‘miniature trees’ much like the rheophyte S. cuprea) and shows xerophytic adaptation, the leafy sprays curling inwards as the plant dries up but rehydrating to regain the extended flattened condition in moister conditions

Malay Pen. (1966) 2024--2025) records various species used in poulticing or for decoctions drunk as post-childbirth tonics and for stomach aches, rheumatism or asthma, but the species may not be identified precisely
He also records the use of the readily identifiable S. willdenowii in infusions given for high fever.

Among the extant Lycopsida, the Selaginellaceae are distinguished from the Lycopodiaceae by ligulate microphylls and the heterosporous condition, and from the Isoetaceae by biflagellate (rather than multiflagellate) sperm and the lack of secondary growth
Subgenus Selaginella, with spirally arranged, essentially monomorphic leaves, is of predominantly temperate distribution
Subgenus Heterophyllum Hieron., with leaves in four ranks along the branch axes, is mainly tropical and the only group encountered in Peninsular Malaysia

The latter subgenus in Peninsular Malaysia appears to be naturally divided as Section Homostachyeae (with monomorphic sporophylls and cylindric-quadrangular strobili) and Section Heterostachyeae (with dimorphic sporophylls and bilaterally symmetrical strobili) in the system of Ridley (1919), who gave the first account of Selaginella in the Malay Peninsula, listing 37 species
Alston (1934) reduced this number to 25, and by the time of his Sumatran account (1937), the Peninsular Malaysian tally was 26 species
Wong (1983) enumerated 28 species and pointed out groups of related species by sets of shared morphological characters
Selaginella pubescens is added through the present account
Selaginella siamensis Hieron. in Parris & Latiff (1997) is S. frondosa.
